title: Graph is a Substrate Across Data Modalities
one_liner: Reuse the same learned graph structure across different tasks and data types instead of building a new graph each time.
lead: When you have multiple tasks (like recognizing faces, reading text, understanding social networks), each one builds its own internal graph of relationships. But this wastes learning—the basic patterns that make a good graph (which things connect, how strongly) are the same across all three. This paper argues that graph structure should be built once and reused as a shared foundation, the way a building's wiring infrastructure serves all the rooms inside.

problem.h2: Every task learns graphs from scratch
paras: Machine learning models process information by finding which pieces matter and how they relate. A graph is just a way to encode those relationships: nodes (like people or words) and edges (like friendships or word co-occurrences). When you train a model to solve a task, part of what it does is figure out the structure—which nodes should connect to which others.

The problem: when a new task comes along (say, you learned to recognize faces, now you need to translate speech), the model builds a completely new graph. It throws away everything it learned about structure and starts over. Across ten tasks, you build ten separate graphs. But here is the waste: the underlying relational patterns—how densely things cluster, which nodes act as hubs—are often the same. You keep reconstructing the same pattern over and over.

callout.html: Instead of learning a new graph for each task, keep one graph and train it to work across all tasks simultaneously.

panels.title: 1. The old way
panels.caption: Three tasks build three separate graphs, each rebuilt from nothing.

panels.title: 2. Wasteful rebuild
panels.caption: Same structure discovered three times independently (waste).

panels.title: 3. Shared substrate
panels.caption: One graph learned jointly from all three tasks at once.

panels.title: 4. Role-based training
panels.viz_args: Task A: link predictor | Task B: feature reducer | Task C: classifier
panels.caption: Same graph used as different parts (predictor, reducer, classifier).

panels.title: 5. Payoff
panels.caption: Shared graph reaches better accuracy faster, knows more from less data.

steps.b: Step 1: Design a unified structure schema
steps.text: Define a single graph vocabulary (node types, edge types) that all tasks can use.

steps.b: Step 2: Train on all tasks together
steps.text: Feed data from all tasks to the same graph simultaneously.

In round one, the graph acts as a link predictor (guess which nodes connect). In round two, it acts as a feature compressor (reduce noise). In round three, it acts as a classifier (sort into categories).
Feedback from all three roles adjusts the same edges and nodes simultaneously.
Over training, the graph hardens into a structure that serves all three purposes well.

paras: The paper modifies the graph structure itself—which nodes exist, which pairs are connected, how strong each edge is. Instead of learning a task-specific graph, it learns one shared graph that all tasks point to.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: task-invariant structure score
hidden.name: Structural alignment across tasks
paras: The paper measures something that never appears explicitly but drives the results: how much the learned graph is the same across all tasks. If every task learns a wildly different graph, the score is low. If all tasks converge on the same structure (same clusters, same hubs), the score is high.

The paper does not directly report this number, but it estimates it implicitly. When it trains the graph on multiple tasks together and updates all edges based on feedback from all tasks, it is measuring how stable the graph is. A stable structure means many tasks agree on which edges matter; an unstable one means tasks pull in opposite directions. By observing final accuracy, the paper infers backward: if a shared graph wins, then there must be significant task-invariant structure hiding in the data.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger evidence that structure is reusable across tasks.

reads.html: The paper's results show that one shared graph outperforms three separate graphs, because when feedback from multiple tasks adjusts the same edges simultaneously, edges that serve many tasks get stronger while edges only one task needs fade away. The hidden quantity is that overlap—how much the tasks agree on what the graph should look like.

The paper reports accuracy, data efficiency, and generalization gains, but the mechanism behind them is structural alignment. A graph that works for multiple tasks must encode commonalities in how data is organized across those tasks. The interleaved role-based training forces the graph to optimize for this alignment.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: shared learning compresses redundancy
paras: Here is the core reason this works. When you train one graph on ten tasks together, each task sends feedback (gradient) to every edge. If an edge is useful for task A and useless for task B, the gradients will partly cancel out—the edge stays near a middle ground. But if an edge is useful for many tasks, all their gradients reinforce it. Over training, edges that serve multiple purposes strengthen, and edges that only mattered for one task fade. The final graph ends up encoding the patterns all tasks share.

The role-based training accelerates this. In round one, the graph learns to predict missing links—which node pairs are most likely to connect. This teaches it to find the backbone structure (clusters and hubs). In round two, it learns to remove noise, which refines that structure. In round three, it learns to sort examples into categories, which fine-tunes the structure for prediction. By using the same graph in three different ways, the method forces it to be flexible and general. A graph that only learned to predict links would be brittle; one that has been used as a link-predictor, a denoiser, and a classifier is resilient.

stages.s: Unified schema: map each modality to nodes and edges
Gradients from all rounds reinforce shared structure
One resilient graph for all tasks

math.words: total error equals the sum of errors from all tasks, weighted equally, minus a penalty term that encourages different tasks to agree on the graph structure
math.equation: L_total = sum_task L_task(G, theta_task) + lambda * D_align(G_1, G_2, ..., G_k)
symbols: the total error the model tries to minimize
the error for one single task (the gap between guess and true answer)
the shared graph: all its edges and their strengths
the task-specific weights (the part not shared)
how much to reward the tasks for agreeing on structure (a number you choose)
a measure of how different the tasks want G to be (low if they agree, high if they disagree)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Task A alone: error 8.0 (a big gap between guesses and truth).
When trained together on one graph: errors drop to 5.2 + 4.8 + 5.5 = 15.5 (because they share structure).
Alignment bonus (how much the three tasks agree on the graph): D_align = 2.0 (low = high agreement).
Final loss: 15.5 + 1.0 = 16.5 (even lower than the sum of errors from a fully joint model, because it actively encourages agreement).
Gain: isolated 21.5 → joint 16.5, a 23% improvement from reuse.

math.note: The equation says: minimize the combined error from all tasks, but reward the model if all tasks learn similar graph structure.

charts.title: Separate graphs (old way)
charts.note: Each task builds its own graph from scratch, learning is fast but accuracy plateaus.

charts.title: G-Substrate (this paper)
charts.note: One graph for all tasks, reusing structure. Accuracy improves because tasks teach each other.

items.html: If two tasks need fundamentally different graph structures (one wants a densely connected graph, the other wants sparse), the shared graph becomes a compromise that serves neither well. The method assumes significant structural overlap; if that assumption breaks, the shared approach fails.

The unified structural schema has to be designed to fit all modalities. If a new modality arrives (say, a different type of link or node property), the schema might not accommodate it without retraining the whole graph. Rigid schemas limit flexibility.
Running the graph in three different roles sequentially triples the training time compared to a single pass. If data is huge or compute is scarce, this overhead can be prohibitive.

When tasks share genuine structural patterns (like social networks and recommendation graphs both exploiting user similarity), G-Substrate shines, because each task's learning step refines the shared graph in a direction that helps the other tasks too, so feedback from all tasks adds up rather than cancels out.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small multi-task scenario with two or three related tasks (e.g., predict links in a social network AND classify user types AND recommend content—all use the same user-interaction graph). Train G-Substrate's shared graph on all three. In parallel, train three isolated graphs, one per task. Measure the final accuracy of each approach and how many training examples each needed to reach a target accuracy.
demo.metric_eq: Data efficiency gain = (examples_for_isolated_graph_to_reach_80%) minus (examples_for_shared_graph_to_reach_80%), divided by (examples_for_isolated)
demo.closing: The demo must show that the shared graph reaches the same accuracy with fewer examples than any isolated graph (because each example teaches all three tasks at once instead of one task at a time), and that all three tasks improve when they share structure.
